name: Victor Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual lineworker day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and still on the electricity company’s power line repair crew, experienced but not a supervisor. My apprenticeship taught me to check a work order at the pole, and I use AI every day to sort outage reports before we drive out. I like a difficult fault that makes the whole crew think; I dislike a deadline that starts before we have isolated the line. My partner and I have grown children, and I have begun thinking about leaving full-time climbing around sixty-four if the income permits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that modest AI still saves us time at the depot, even if the grand predictions fail. An AI outage list can sort the calls; the broken power line still has to be found at the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Higher lineworker pay, more than six months saved and plenty of nearby jobs make our next few years secure. I want to check retirement income before leaving full-time work around sixty-four; the software itself does not force a decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the repair rota and compare the daily AI outage list with the crew’s site findings. This year I would ask for an updated retirement income estimate and review it with my partner alongside our spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about pay and work. I would enjoy the minutes saved at the depot, provided nobody closes a fault before a crew tests it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When does a sorted list mislead you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two calls may sound like one fault until we test opposite sides of a junction. I split the entries in the tool so the next crew does not drive to the wrong pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your sixty-four plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the estimate does not cover our living costs, I would keep working safely and compare real nearby line jobs. I would not turn a hoped-for date into a promise to my partner.

say: I would **use** AI to sort outage reports while crews still locate and test physical faults.
I would **keep** work orders open until a line test confirms the repair.
think: **Higher** pay, strong savings and many nearby jobs make present income secure.
**Full-time** retirement around sixty-four remains conditional on a real income estimate.
do: **Keep** repair rota and compare AI outage list with site findings.
**Request** retirement income estimate and review it with partner.
feel: **Calm** about income and pleased with modest depot time savings.
S0.quote: An AI outage list can sort the calls; the broken power line still has to be found at the pole.
fieldNote: His **daily** AI use supports routine sorting while field tests retain authority.
**Strong** savings and nearby jobs make a conditional retirement discussion possible without urgency.

steps.text: Keep repair rota and compare AI outage list with site findings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that AI buying and booking could speed a storm response if crews can correct bad part lists. I would ask our union technology group to keep an open record of those corrections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office work changes first, while line repairs still take hands. I expect my own hours to stay steady for now, but fewer junior hires would leave older crews without people learning the fault work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test the new part list against our last ten repair sheets during paid hours and learn its correction form. In the first year I would take the mismatches to the union technology group and ask the company to show when each correction reaches dispatch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for my own wages, and concerned for the next crew. A part list is useful only when the worker who finds its mistake can fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mismatch would matter most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A clamp that fits an AI drawing can still be wrong for the measured conductor on a power line. I would attach the measurement and the work order to the correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why involve the union instead of telling the store yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the store too, but our union group can track whether corrections actually reach every shift. One worker’s private message is easy to lose.

say: I would **test** AI part lists against field repair sheets.
Our **union** group should track whether corrections reach every shift.
think: **Office** tasks change first, while my own physical repair hours look stable.
**Fewer** junior hires could weaken future crews even if I keep earning.
do: **Learn** part-list correction form while testing ten repair sheets on paid time.
**Bring** mismatches to union technology group in the first year.
feel: **Calm** about my income, with concern for apprentices and error tracking.
S1.quote: A clamp that fits an AI drawing can still be wrong for the measured conductor on a power line.
fieldNote: He **sees** paid testing as an extension of daily tool use, not a move out of the trade.
His **union** interest concerns shared error records and future junior training, not personal job panic.

steps.text: Learn AI part-list correction form on paid repair review
Bring ten repair mismatches to union technology group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2028 could make the fault plan when I am sixty, and capable line robots around 2031 could act on it when I am sixty-three. A robot at my last power line callout should have a stop control the crew is paid to use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope to leave full-time climbing around sixty-four if the figures work, so a robot at sixty-three could take the last year of good callout pay. Our strong savings and nearby line jobs give choices, but losing that higher wage would still change the retirement sum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our union group this year for a paid robot stop-work agreement and apply for a company field trial if the crew has that authority. In the first year after 2028 I would learn the robot stop controls on paid time and compare my actual callout earnings with the retirement estimate before moving the finish date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the speed and the final year of earnings, though I have room to act. I do not want a trial where the crew is responsible but cannot stop the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you press stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot grip on a cracked crossarm would be enough. I would photograph the damage, halt the machine and record who authorised any restart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at sixty-three instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if an updated income estimate covers our household costs and callout pay has actually fallen. Otherwise I would keep safe field shifts or seek a written nearby offer.

say: **Full** thinking AI in 2028 and line robots around 2031 could shorten my last working years.
I would **seek** paid crew stop authority before robot field trials.
think: A **robot** at sixty-three might cut the final year of higher callout pay I hoped to earn.
**Savings** and nearby work provide choices but do not replace the retirement income figure.
do: **Ask** union group for paid robot stop-work agreement this year.
**Learn** robot stop controls on paid field trial after 2028 if crew can halt machine.
**Compare** actual callout earnings with retirement estimate before changing finish date.
feel: **Anxious** about possible income loss, with savings and local options for response.
S2.quote: A robot at my last power line callout should have a stop control the crew is paid to use.
fieldNote: He does **not** assume an early exit; the future callout loss must be real and the income sufficient.
His **field** trial depends on paid time and explicit stop authority, despite his willingness to adopt early.

steps.text: Ask union technology group for paid robot stop-work agreement
Learn robot stop controls on paid trial if crew has stop authority
Bring full-time finish to sixty-three only if income covers costs and callouts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that thinking AI by 2031 changes dispatch when I am sixty-three, while capable robots around 2034 arrive after my hoped-for full-time finish. The company has time to teach younger workers to check a machine plan against the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our retirement estimate covers living costs at sixty-four, I could leave full-time climbing before robots arrive. A depot farewell is not worth much if the power line retirement figures leave a hole in our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the training office about paid field-check shifts for experienced lineworkers and request an updated retirement estimate. If a posted checking role has enough pay and I still need income after sixty-four, I would apply in the first year after 2031; otherwise I would keep regular repairs until the household figures work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about the technology dates, with a little uncertainty about our own retirement sums. The extra years let me choose from real pay offers rather than a rushed guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the younger workers check in a machine plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They should compare the pole tag, isolation boundary and damaged hardware with the proposed repair. I would make them explain any mismatch before a robot moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would a field checking job need to pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough to close the gap between the retirement estimate and our actual bills. I would ask for written hours and a wage before leaving the repair rota.

say: The 2034 **robot** date may fall after my conditional full-time finish.
I would **teach** workers to compare robot plans with real pole tags.
think: **Retirement** income may be enough by sixty-four, but a shortfall would require paid field work.
An **actual** checking offer matters more than a ceremonial exit.
do: **Request** retirement estimate and paid field-check job terms this year.
**Apply** after 2031 if posted field-check role covers retirement income gap.
**Keep** regular repairs until household income suffices or suitable role appears.
feel: **Mostly** calm about dates, with some uncertainty about retirement income.
S3.quote: A depot farewell is not worth much if the power line retirement figures leave a hole in our bills.
fieldNote: He **distinguishes** a planned finish from a guarantee of enough retirement income.
The **fallback** field-check job depends on a posted offer with written pay and hours.

steps.text: Apply after 2031 if posted field-check role covers retirement income gap
Keep repair shifts until retirement income or suitable paid role suffices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI by 2036 and line robots around 2039 give apprentices time to learn real faults before the machine reaches the pole. I would put my experience into paid practice days while I am still working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight for thinking AI and seventy-one for robots, I may have left full-time work if our sixty-four plan proves affordable. I would still want the next crew to know when an AI fault map is wrong; that does not require me to promise unpaid regular teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the company this year for paid apprentice practice days and keep my current repair shifts. If the company offers them at my usual rate, I would teach one day each quarter while still employed; if our retirement estimate covers costs at sixty-four, I would then finish full-time on the existing plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, because the machine date is beyond the period I hope to be climbing. I can use the time to leave a better set of field habits with younger workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an apprentice practice on the first day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An apprentice should be allowed to prove an AI outage map wrong before a line robot follows it. They should show their reason, not guess what the screen wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep teaching after full-time work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might take an occasional paid session if the hours suit us, but I would decide then. I would not count possible teaching money in our retirement budget now.

say: A **decade** allows paid field practice before line robots reach poles around 2039.
I would **teach** apprentices to challenge AI fault maps with real measurements.
think: I **may** have left full-time climbing before AI arrives if the income plan works.
**Occasional** future teaching is possible but not guaranteed household income.
do: **Request** paid apprentice practice days and keep repair shifts now.
**Teach** one quarterly field day if offered at usual rate while employed.
**Finish** full-time at planned sixty-four only if retirement income covers costs.
feel: **Calm** about later robots and able to pass on field skills.
S4.quote: An apprentice should be allowed to prove an AI outage map wrong before a line robot follows it.
fieldNote: He **wants** paid teaching during existing employment, not a second unpaid career.
The **planned** sixty-four exit remains conditional on retirement income, not a new early-retirement choice.

steps.text: Keep repairs and request paid apprentice practice days
Teach quarterly field day if paid usual rate while employed
Finish full-time at planned sixty-four if retirement income covers costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because line robots could reach repairs when I am sixty-three, one year before my hoped-for full-time finish. Paid stop authority and an honest account of callout hours would help. I will learn a robot control, but I will not let a power line trial hide who is responsible for a bad repair.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets to read the robot trial failure record. The next line crew and the apprentices need it, even if the company would rather show a successful film. A worker should be paid to record a mistake before anyone repeats it.

headlineQuote: I will learn a robot control, but I will not let a power line trial hide who is responsible for a bad repair.
portrait: **Victor** is a fifty-eight-year-old electricity company lineworker with a vocational certificate, apprenticeship and daily AI use for outage reports.
**Higher** pay, more than six months saved and plenty of nearby jobs support his partner and grown children as retirement nears.
He **wants** union-backed error records and paid crew stop authority, while accepting tools early when field workers can correct them.
He **hopes** to finish full-time around sixty-four if income permits; the fast robot date could threaten his final year of callout pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring line robots around 2031, one year before his tentative full-time finish.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** crew stop authority and clear callout earnings records would let him judge any income gap.
